title: Sentiment Analysis
shortDefinition: An AI technique that determines the emotional tone or attitude expressed in text.
definition: Sentiment analysis is an AI technique that determines the emotional tone or attitude expressed in text — typically classifying content as positive, negative, or neutral, and sometimes detecting more nuanced emotions like frustration, satisfaction, or urgency. Businesses use sentiment analysis to process large volumes of customer feedback, support tickets, reviews, and social media mentions at a scale manual review can't match.

sections.title: How sentiment analysis works
sections.description: Sentiment analysis models classify text as positive, negative, or neutral, often with aspect-level detection.

content.text: Sentiment analysis models — ranging from simpler lexicon-based approaches (scoring text based on known positive/negative words) to modern transformer-based classifiers and LLMs — analyze text and assign a sentiment label or score. More sophisticated systems detect sentiment at the aspect level (identifying that a review is positive about a product's quality but negative about shipping speed), rather than producing a single overall sentiment score for an entire piece of text, which is significantly more useful for actionable business insight.

content.title: Types of sentiment analysis:
items: Binary classification: positive vs. negative.
Ternary classification: positive, negative, or neutral.
Fine-grained scoring: numerical sentiment score (e.g., -1 to +1).
Emotion detection: identifies specific emotions (anger, joy, frustration).
Aspect-based sentiment: sentiment toward specific features or topics.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Sentiment analysis turns unstructured feedback into structured data at scale — identifying patterns in customer emotion that manual review would miss.

sections.title: Common business applications of sentiment analysis

content.text: Sentiment analysis powers customer support prioritization (routing frustrated or urgent customers for faster response), brand monitoring (tracking sentiment trends across social media and review platforms), product feedback analysis (identifying specific features customers love or dislike), and employee feedback analysis (surfacing morale trends from survey responses at scale). The common thread is processing a volume of text feedback too large for manual review while still extracting actionable, specific insight rather than just an aggregate 'mostly positive' summary.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of sentiment analysis

content.text: Sentiment analysis has significant limitations. It struggles with sarcasm, irony, and nuanced tone that humans easily detect. Domain-specific language and industry jargon can reduce accuracy, and context dependency (the same phrase can be positive or negative depending on context) is a common failure mode. Aggregating sentiment across documents can mask important variation, and models trained on one domain often perform poorly on another.

items: Sarcasm and irony: models often misinterpret non-literal language.
Domain specificity: industry jargon can confuse generic models.
Context dependency: the same phrase can have different sentiment in different contexts.
Aggregation masks variation: overall scores hide important differences.
Language limitations: multilingual sentiment analysis is still challenging.
Emotion nuance: basic sentiment misses complex emotional states.
Bias: models can have inherent biases from training data.

content.title: Important
content.text: Sentiment analysis is most valuable when combined with human review for edge cases and validation — never rely on automated sentiment alone for critical decisions.

sections.title: Best practices for sentiment analysis implementation

content.text: Implementing sentiment analysis effectively requires careful domain tuning, validation, and integration with human review. The following practices can help ensure your sentiment analysis delivers actionable insights.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Define your sentiment categories clearly (positive/negative/neutral or more nuanced).
Build a representative test set from your actual text data.
Validate sentiment accuracy on your domain-specific vocabulary.
Consider aspect-level detection for more actionable insights.
Implement confidence scoring for uncertain classifications.
Set up human review for low-confidence or high-stakes sentiment.
Monitor sentiment trends over time, not just individual scores.
Plan for periodic model retraining as language and customer sentiment evolve.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure accuracy on a domain-specific test set — generic accuracy benchmarks often don't reflect real-world performance on your specific content.

items.question: What is aspect-based sentiment analysis?
items.answer: Aspect-based sentiment analysis identifies sentiment toward specific features or topics within a single piece of text. For example, 'The camera is excellent but the battery life is terrible' — positive on 'camera,' negative on 'battery life.'

items.question: What is the difference between sentiment analysis and emotion detection?
items.answer: Sentiment analysis typically classifies polarity (positive/negative/neutral). Emotion detection goes further, identifying specific emotional states like anger, joy, frustration, or satisfaction. Emotion detection is more nuanced but also more challenging.

items.question: Can sentiment analysis work with very short text like tweets or chat messages?
items.answer: Yes, though short text can be challenging due to limited context. Models can still identify sentiment from word choice and emojis, but accuracy may be lower than with longer, more contextual text.

items.question: How do I choose between sentiment analysis and manual feedback review?
items.answer: Sentiment analysis is for scale — processing thousands or millions of feedback items. Manual review is for depth — understanding specific cases in detail. Most organizations use both: sentiment analysis for broad trends, manual review for validation and edge cases.
